title: A learning path, from counts to tissue
text:
New to omics analysis? Follow the modules in order. Each one builds on the ideas of the one before. If you already know the basics, jump straight to the module you need.
0

title: Count matrix
text:
The table almost every omics analysis starts from. Rows are genes; columns are samples (bulk RNA-seq) or single cells (single-cell RNA-seq). Each number counts how many sequencing reads or molecules came from that gene. Example: GAPDH has 5,200 reads in a tumour sample and 4,900 in a normal sample. Those are two entries of the matrix. A bulk study is often ~20,000 genes × 6–50 samples; a single-cell study is ~20,000 genes × tens of thousands of cells, mostly zeros.
See it in Module 1 →

title: Sample metadata
text:
A second table with one row per sample (or cell) that says where each column came from: the condition, genotype, sex, age, tissue, the animal or patient, and how it was processed (date, kit, sequencing lane). The analysis can only compare what the metadata records. Example: Trt_2 · treated · mouse M5 · batch 2. If the treatment is not written down, it cannot be tested.
See it in Module 1 →

title: Biological replicates vs. technical batches
text:
A biological replicate is an independent unit: a different mouse, patient or separately grown culture. Replicates capture natural variation, and you need several per group (usually three or more) to tell a real difference from chance. Re-sequencing the same RNA, or cutting two sections from one tumour, does not add a replicate. A technical batch is a set of samples processed together (same day, kit lot, lane or slide), which can shift them all in the same direction. Example: 3 control and 3 treated mice are 6 replicates. If all controls were prepared on Monday and all treated mice on Tuesday, the day effect and the treatment effect cannot be separated.
See it in Module 2 →

title: Normalisation
text:
Adjusting raw counts so samples can be compared fairly, because they receive different numbers of reads and differ in RNA make-up. Example: sample A is sequenced to 20 million reads and sample B to 40 million. Every gene in B has about twice the counts even though nothing biological changed. Dividing by library size (counts per million) fixes this. TMM also corrects for a few very highly expressed genes using up the reads. In single-cell data each cell is scaled to the same total, e.g. 10,000, then log-transformed.
See it in Module 1 →

title: Experimental design
text:
The plan of which samples you have and which comparisons you will make, written for the analysis as a model formula. It is decided before sequencing: enough replicates, groups spread across batches, every variable recorded. Example: ~ batch + condition asks "what does the condition change, after allowing for batch?". For before-and-after samples from the same patients, ~ patient + condition compares each patient with themselves.
See it in Module 1 →

title: How RNA-seq evolved
text:
Each step changed what a single experiment can measure: one gene, then thousands, then every transcript, then every cell, then every cell in place. The statistics changed with it. limma started on microarrays and was adapted to counts.
1977
One gene at a time

title: Northern blot
text:
RNA separated on a gel and probed for a single known gene. Slow, low throughput, but the first way to see expression levels directly.
1995
Thousands of genes

title: Microarrays and SAGE
text:
cDNA microarrays (Schena et al.) and SAGE measured thousands of known transcripts at once. Arrays could only detect what was printed on them and lost accuracy at very low or very high expression.
2004
Statistics

title: limma and empirical Bayes
text:
Gordon Smyth's limma "borrowed strength" across genes to stabilise variance estimates when you only have a few replicates. That idea is still at the heart of the pipeline below.
2008
Sequencing arrives

title: RNA-seq
text:
Short-read sequencing of cDNA (Mortazavi et al. in mouse, Nagalakshmi et al. in yeast) counted transcripts directly. It needs no probes, has a wider dynamic range, and finds novel transcripts and splice junctions.
2010
Count statistics

title: edgeR, DESeq and TMM
text:
Counts are not continuous, so new models used the negative binomial distribution. Robinson and Oshlack introduced TMM normalisation, showing that dividing by library size alone gives biased results.
2009–13
Resolution

title: Single-cell RNA-seq
text:
Tang et al. sequenced a single cell's transcriptome in 2009. By 2013 Nature Methods named single-cell sequencing its Method of the Year. The STAR aligner (2013) made fast spliced alignment routine.
2014
Statistics

title: voom and DESeq2
text:
voom (Law et al.) converted counts to log-CPM with precision weights, so limma's linear models could be used on RNA-seq. DESeq2 was published the same year. Both are still standard.
2015–17
Scale and speed

title: Droplets and pseudo-alignment
text:
Drop-seq and inDrop, then the 10x Chromium, profiled thousands of cells per run. kallisto and Salmon quantified transcripts in minutes, without full alignment.
2016–20
Location and length

title: Spatial and long-read RNA
text:
Spatial transcriptomics (Ståhl et al., 2016) kept tissue position; Nature Methods made it Method of the Year 2020. Nanopore direct RNA and PacBio Iso-Seq read full-length isoforms. nf-core made pipelines reproducible across clusters and clouds.
2023–26
Now

title: Multi-million cells, isoforms and models
text: Long-read isoform quantification is affordable at scale, single-cell atlases reach tens of millions of cells, and spatial panels now cover thousands of genes. Bulk RNA-seq is still the most common design for comparing conditions, because it is cheap, deep and well understood.

title: RNA-seq types: advantages and limitations
text:
| Assay | What it measures | Advantages | Limitations | Typical analysis
| Bulk poly(A) mRNA | Average expression of coding genes in a sample | Cheap, deep, mature tooling, easy to replicate | Averages over cell types; needs intact RNA (RIN ≥ 7) | limma-voom, edgeR, DESeq2
| Bulk total RNA (rRNA-depleted) | Coding and non-coding RNA, including pre-mRNA | Works on degraded and FFPE RNA; captures lncRNA | More reads needed; intronic reads complicate counting | Same as above
| 3′ tag-seq (QuantSeq, BRB-seq) | One read per transcript near the 3′ end | Very low cost per sample; good for large screens | No isoform or splicing information | limma-voom, edgeR
| Single-cell / single-nucleus | Expression in each cell | Resolves cell types and states | Sparse counts, dissociation artefacts, higher cost | Seurat, Scanpy; pseudobulk + limma/edgeR for DE
| Spatial | Expression with tissue coordinates | Keeps neighbourhood context | Panel limits or bin resolution; expensive | See Module 3
| Long-read (PacBio, Nanopore) | Full-length isoforms; direct RNA can detect modifications | Isoform-level answers, fusion transcripts | Lower depth per dollar; tools still maturing | IsoQuant, bambu, FLAIR + DTU tests

title: Why TMM normalisation matters
text:
A sequencer gives each sample a fixed budget of reads. If a few genes become hugely expressed in one sample, they use up a larger share of that budget, and every other gene gets fewer reads, even though its real expression did not change. Dividing by total library size (CPM) does not fix this, so unchanged genes look down-regulated.
TMM (trimmed mean of M-values) assumes most genes are not differentially expressed. For each sample against a reference sample it:
computes each gene's log-ratio M and average abundance A;
trims the most extreme 30% of M values and 5% of A values;
takes a precision-weighted mean of what is left;
turns that into a scaling factor, so the effective library size is lib.size × norm.factor.
Try it: increase the share of strongly up-regulated genes and compare the two modes. With CPM, the cloud of unchanged grey genes slides below zero. TMM moves it back to zero.
Now push the slider past about 30%. TMM fails too, because its core assumption (most genes unchanged) no longer holds. Global shifts like this happen in some experiments, such as transcriptional amplification by MYC. They need spike-in controls rather than TMM.
MA plot: x = average log-expression, y = log₂ fold change B vs A. Grey = unchanged genes; magenta = truly up in B. Green dashed line = median of the unchanged genes.
Unchanged genes, median log₂FC0.00
TMM factor, B relative to A1.00
| Method | Normalisation | Model | Best when
| limma-voom | TMM (edgeR) | Linear model on log-CPM with precision weights | Complex designs, many samples, fast; strong for gene-set tests

title: Why TMM normalisation matters
text:
| edgeR quasi-likelihood | TMM | Negative binomial GLM | Small samples, low counts
| DESeq2 | Median-of-ratios | Negative binomial GLM with shrunken fold changes | Small studies wanting stable fold-change estimates

title: From FASTQ files to a count matrix
text:
limma-voom starts from a gene-by-sample table of raw read counts. For your own data, produce it with nf-core/rnaseq: trimming, STAR alignment, Salmon quantification and full QC (FastQC, RSeQC, MultiQC) in one command. It runs locally, on a cluster, or on AWS.
Shell
# samplesheet.csv: sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.19.0 \
-profile docker \
--input samplesheet.csv \
--genome GRCm39 \
--aligner star_salmon \
--outdir results
# counts for limma: results/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv
# on AWS: add -profile awsbatch or launch the same workflow on AWS HealthOmics
Don't Never feed TPM or FPKM values into limma or edgeR. They need raw counts. With Salmon output, import via tximport(..., countsFromAbundance = "lengthScaledTPM"), which gives count-scale values that limma-voom accepts.
Version Pin the pipeline with -r for reproducibility. Check the latest release on the nf-core website before you run.

title: Download GSE63310 and build a DGEList
text:
A DGEList holds three things together: the counts, the sample table (library size, group, normalisation factor) and the gene annotation.
R
url <- "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?acc=GSE63310&format=file"
download.file(url, destfile = "GSE63310_RAW.tar", mode = "wb")
untar("GSE63310_RAW.tar", exdir = ".")
files <- c("GSM1545535_10_6_5_11.txt", "GSM1545536_9_6_5_11.txt",
"GSM1545538_purep53.txt", "GSM1545539_JMS8-2.txt",
"GSM1545540_JMS8-3.txt", "GSM1545541_JMS8-4.txt",
"GSM1545542_JMS8-5.txt", "GSM1545544_JMS9-P7c.txt",
"GSM1545545_JMS9-P8c.txt")
for (f in paste0(files, ".gz")) R.utils::gunzip(f, overwrite = TRUE)
x <- readDGE(files, columns = c(1, 3)) # col 1 = Entrez ID, col 3 = count
colnames(x) <- substring(colnames(x), 12) # drop the GSM prefix
dim(x)
[1] 27179 9

title: Add sample groups, batch and gene annotation
text:
The cell type is the biology. The sequencing lane is a technical batch you will put in the model. Gene symbols make results readable.
R
group <- factor(c("LP","ML","Basal","Basal","ML","LP","Basal","ML","LP"))
lane <- factor(rep(c("L004", "L006", "L008"), c(3, 4, 2)))
x$samples$group <- group
x$samples$lane <- lane
genes <- AnnotationDbi::select(org.Mm.eg.db, keys = rownames(x),
columns = c("SYMBOL", "GENENAME"), keytype = "ENTREZID")
genes <- genes[!duplicated(genes$ENTREZID), ]
x$genes <- genes
x$samples
Design check Every group appears on more than one lane, so lane and cell type are not confounded. If a batch matched a group exactly, no statistical method could separate them.

title: Remove lowly expressed genes
text:
Genes with almost no reads cannot be tested and add noise to the mean-variance trend. filterByExpr() keeps genes with enough counts in at least as many samples as the smallest group, scaled to library size.
R
table(rowSums(x$counts == 0) == 9) # genes with zero counts everywhere
keep <- filterByExpr(x, group = group)
x <- x[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # recalculate library sizes
dim(x)
# density of log-CPM before vs after filtering
lcpm <- cpm(x, log = TRUE)
plotDensities(lcpm, legend = FALSE, main = "After filtering")
[1] 16624 9

title: TMM normalisation
text:
calcNormFactors() computes one factor per sample. It does not change the counts; it stores factors that every downstream function (cpm, voom) uses automatically. Factors are scaled so they multiply to 1.
R
x <- calcNormFactors(x, method = "TMM")
round(x$samples$norm.factors, 3)
x$samples$lib.size * x$samples$norm.factors # effective library sizes
# teaching exercise: distort two samples and watch TMM correct them
x2 <- x
x2$samples$norm.factors <- 1
x2$counts[, 1] <- ceiling(x2$counts[, 1] * 0.05)
x2$counts[, 2] <- x2$counts[, 2] * 5
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(cpm(x2, log = TRUE), las = 2, main = "Unnormalised")
x2 <- calcNormFactors(x2)
boxplot(cpm(x2, log = TRUE), las = 2, main = "TMM-normalised")
[1] 0.894 1.025 1.046 1.046 1.016 0.922 0.996 1.086 0.984
Read it These factors are all close to 1, so composition bias is mild here. Factors outside about 0.5–2 point to a problem sample, very different RNA composition, or contamination. Investigate before you continue.
Newer For data with many zeros (low-input or degraded samples), method = "TMMwsp" (TMM with singleton pairing) is more stable. In edgeR 4, normLibSizes() is the new name for calcNormFactors(); both work.

title: Check sample relationships with MDS
text:
Before testing anything, see whether samples group by biology. The first dimension should separate cell types; if they group by lane instead, the batch effect is strong.
R
lcpm <- cpm(x, log = TRUE) # now TMM-aware
col.group <- c("#C2410C", "#2563EB", "#16865A")[as.integer(group)]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotMDS(lcpm, labels = group, col = col.group, main = "A. Cell type")
plotMDS(lcpm, labels = lane, dim.plot = c(3, 4), main = "B. Lane (dims 3 & 4)")
glimmaMDS(x, groups = x$samples[, c("group", "lane")]) # interactive HTML

title: Design matrix and contrasts
text:
The design has one column per cell type (no intercept) plus lane as a batch term. Contrasts then name the comparisons you care about.
R
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group + lane)
colnames(design) <- gsub("group", "", colnames(design))
contr.matrix <- makeContrasts(
BasalvsLP = Basal - LP,
BasalvsML = Basal - ML,
LPvsML = LP - ML,
levels = colnames(design))
contr.matrix
Batch Model batch in the design, as here. removeBatchEffect() is only for plots and heatmaps; never test DE on batch-removed values.

title: voom, linear model and empirical Bayes
text:
voom converts counts to log-CPM using the TMM-adjusted library sizes. It then estimates how variance depends on expression level and gives each observation a precision weight. limma fits a weighted linear model per gene, and eBayes shrinks gene variances towards a common trend.
R
v <- voom(x, design, plot = TRUE) # mean–variance trend should be smooth
vfit <- lmFit(v, design)
vfit <- contrasts.fit(vfit, contrasts = contr.matrix)
efit <- eBayes(vfit)
plotSA(efit, main = "Final model: mean-variance trend")
summary(decideTests(efit))
| FDR 5% | Basal vs LP | Basal vs ML | LP vs ML
| Down | 4,648 | 4,927 | 3,135
| Not significant | 7,113 | 7,026 | 10,972
| Up | 4,863 | 4,671 | 2,517
Variations for other designs
R
# some samples noisier than others: down-weight them
v <- voomWithQualityWeights(x, design, plot = TRUE)
# repeated samples from the same patient (paired / blocked design)
corfit <- duplicateCorrelation(v, design, block = patient)
vfit <- lmFit(v, design, block = patient, correlation = corfit$consensus)
# newer one-step alternative in edgeR (handles zeros better)
vfit <- voomLmFit(x, design, sample.weights = TRUE, plot = TRUE)
# mixed models with several random effects: variancePartition::dream()

title: Rank genes, apply a fold-change threshold and plot
text:
With thousands of significant genes, focus on large effects. treat() tests whether the fold change is above a threshold, which is stricter and more honest than filtering the results by log fold change after the test.
R
tfit <- treat(vfit, lfc = 1) # |log2FC| > 1, i.e. more than 2-fold
dt <- decideTests(tfit)
summary(dt)
basal.vs.lp <- topTreat(tfit, coef = 1, n = Inf)
head(basal.vs.lp[, c("SYMBOL", "logFC", "AveExpr", "adj.P.Val")])
plotMD(tfit, column = 1, status = dt[, 1], main = colnames(tfit)[1], xlim = c(-8, 13))
glimmaMA(tfit, dge = x, coef = 1) # interactive MD plot + per-gene counts
# volcano plot
tt <- topTable(efit, coef = "BasalvsLP", n = Inf)
tt$status <- ifelse(tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & tt$logFC > 1, "Up",
ifelse(tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & tt$logFC < -1, "Down", "NS"))
ggplot(tt, aes(logFC, -log10(P.Value), colour = status)) +
geom_point(size = 0.6) +
scale_colour_manual(values = c(Up = "#C2410C", Down = "#2563EB", NS = "grey70")) +
theme_minimal()
# heatmap of the top 100 genes
top <- rownames(basal.vs.lp)[1:100]
pheatmap(lcpm[top, ], scale = "row", labels_row = x$genes[top, "SYMBOL"],
annotation_col = data.frame(group = group, row.names = colnames(lcpm)),
show_rownames = FALSE)
| treat, |log₂FC| > 1 | Basal vs LP | Basal vs ML | LP vs ML
| Down | 1,632 | 1,777 | 224
| Not significant | 12,976 | 12,790 | 16,210
| Up | 2,016 | 2,057 | 190

title: Gene set testing with camera
text:
camera() tests whether a whole pathway moves together, while accounting for correlation between genes in the set. That correlation is what makes many simpler enrichment tests too optimistic. Here we use MSigDB Hallmark sets mapped to mouse.
R
library(msigdbr)
h <- msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "H") # older msigdbr: category = "H"
idcol <- intersect(c("ncbi_gene", "entrez_gene"), names(h))[1]
sets <- split(as.character(h[[idcol]]), h$gs_name)
idx <- ids2indices(sets, id = rownames(v))
cam <- camera(v, idx, design, contrast = contr.matrix[, "BasalvsLP"])
head(cam, 10)
barcodeplot(efit$t[, "BasalvsLP"],
index = idx[["HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION"]],
main = "Basal vs LP: EMT hallmark")
Also Use fry() for a few hand-picked sets, and goana() / kegga() for over-representation of your DE gene list.

title: GSEA with MSigDB: all genes ranked by the moderated t
text:
Rank every tested gene by limma's moderated t-statistic, which combines fold change, variance and sample size. Then ask whether a gene set's members pile up at the top (up-regulated) or the bottom (down-regulated) of the list. No cut-off is needed, so GSEA detects pathways where many genes shift a little, even if none passes FDR on its own.
R · ranks + gene sets
library(fgsea); library(msigdbr); library(data.table)
# MSigDB collections (msigdbr ≥ 10: collection/subcollection; older: category/subcategory)
# recent msigdbr downloads the gene sets on first use, so that run needs internet
hall <- msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "H")
reac <- msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "C2", subcollection = "CP:REACTOME")
gobp <- msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP")
pathways <- split(hall$gene_symbol, hall$gs_name)
# rank ALL tested genes by the moderated t (from eBayes, step 09)
tt <- topTable(efit, coef = "BasalvsLP", number = Inf)
tt <- tt[!is.na(tt$SYMBOL), ]
tt <- tt[order(-abs(tt$t)), ]; tt <- tt[!duplicated(tt$SYMBOL), ] # one value per symbol
ranks <- sort(setNames(tt$t, tt$SYMBOL), decreasing = TRUE)
R · run GSEA
gsea_all <- fgsea(pathways, ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500)
gsea_all <- gsea_all[order(padj, -abs(NES))]
head(gsea_all[, .(pathway, NES, padj, size)], 10)
fwrite(gsea_all, "BasalvsLP_Hallmark_GSEA_allgenes.tsv", sep = "\t", sep2 = c("", ",", ""))
# running-score plot for the top set
plotEnrichment(pathways[[gsea_all$pathway[1]]], ranks) + ggplot2::ggtitle(gsea_all$pathway[1])

title: GSEA with MSigDB: all genes ranked by the moderated t
text:
# clusterProfiler alternative (same idea, different API)
# clusterProfiler::GSEA(ranks, TERM2GENE = hall[, c("gs_name", "gene_symbol")], eps = 0)
Read it NES > 0: the set is enriched among genes up in Basal; NES < 0: enriched among genes up in LP. Use padj (FDR) < 0.05. The leadingEdge column lists the genes driving the score, which are the ones to plot and follow up.
Why t, not logFC? Ranking by logFC alone lets noisy, low-count genes with large fold changes dominate. The moderated t down-weights them, so it is the usual choice after limma.

title: Significant genes only (adj. P < 0.05): ORA and restricted GSEA
text:
Sometimes you want to ask what your DE gene list is about. With a cut-off list, the standard test is over-representation analysis (ORA). Are up-regulated (or down-regulated) genes found in a set more often than chance, compared with all tested genes? Run up and down separately; pooling them hides direction.
R · ORA of significant genes
library(clusterProfiler)
t2g <- hall[, c("gs_name", "gene_symbol")]
universe <- names(ranks) # every tested gene, not the genome
sig_up <- tt$SYMBOL[tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & tt$logFC > 0]
sig_down <- tt$SYMBOL[tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & tt$logFC < 0]
ora_up <- enricher(sig_up, TERM2GENE = t2g, universe = universe,
minGSSize = 15, maxGSSize = 500)
ora_down <- enricher(sig_down, TERM2GENE = t2g, universe = universe,
minGSSize = 15, maxGSSize = 500)
head(as.data.frame(ora_up)[, c("ID", "GeneRatio", "BgRatio", "p.adjust")])
dotplot(ora_up, showCategory = 15) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Up in Basal: Hallmark ORA")
R · GSEA restricted to significant genes
ranks_sig <- ranks[names(ranks) %in% c(sig_up, sig_down)]
gsea_sig <- fgsea(pathways, ranks_sig, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500)
gsea_sig[order(padj)][1:10, .(pathway, NES, padj, size)]
Read with care When every gene in the list is already significant, GSEA no longer asks "is this pathway changed?". It asks "do this pathway's DE genes lean up or down?". Sets also need ≥ 10 significant members, so many drop out. Use it as a direction summary next to ORA, not as a replacement for the all-genes GSEA.
| Approach | Input | Question answered | Use when

title: Glossary
text:
CPM
Counts per million: counts divided by library size × 10⁶. With TMM, the effective (normalised) library size is used.
TMM
Trimmed mean of M-values: a scaling factor that corrects for differences in RNA composition between samples.
M / A values
M is the log₂ ratio between two samples; A is the average log₂ expression. Together they form an MA plot.
voom
Variance modelling at the observation level: turns counts into log-CPM with precision weights for limma.
Empirical Bayes
Shrinks each gene's variance estimate towards a common trend, giving stable tests with few replicates.
Contrast
A named comparison between model coefficients, for example Basal − LP.
FDR
False discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among genes called significant (Benjamini–Hochberg).
treat
Tests whether the fold change exceeds a threshold, not just whether it differs from zero.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq with Harmony integration and cell-type annotation
text:
How single-cell sequencing developed, which platform to choose, how Harmony removes batch effects without erasing biology, and a full Seurat pipeline on real PBMC data. The pipeline uses LogNormalize (no SCTransform), Harmony integration, and automated annotation with ScType cross-checked against SingleR, with CellTypist as an alternative.
1 · RNA-seq2 · scRNA-seq3 · SpatialVisium HDDNA-seq / WGS
Status: Tested on simulated data pseudobulk (step 14) and CellTypist (step 13) · Not yet run full pipeline on ifnb
Last reviewed 26 October 2026 · Report an issue with this module · All modules

title: How single-cell RNA-seq evolved
text:
In fifteen years the field went from sequencing one cell to sequencing a hundred million. Most of the gains came from new ways to label each cell's RNA with a barcode: tubes, then plates, then droplets, then split-pool chemistry.
2009
First cell

title: Single-cell transcriptome
text:
Tang et al. sequenced the mRNA of a single mouse blastomere. Each cell was handled by hand in its own tube.
2012–14
Plates

title: Smart-seq, CEL-seq, MARS-seq
text:
Plate-based methods processed hundreds of cells, with full-length coverage (Smart-seq2) or early barcoding and UMIs to count molecules exactly (CEL-seq, MARS-seq). Nature Methods named single-cell sequencing Method of the Year 2013.
2015
Droplets

title: Drop-seq and inDrop
text:
Cells were captured in oil droplets with barcoded beads, raising throughput from hundreds to tens of thousands of cells per experiment.
2016–17
Commercial scale

title: 10x Chromium, CITE-seq, split-pool
text:
The 10x Chromium made droplet scRNA-seq a standard kit. CITE-seq added surface proteins to the same cells. SPLiT-seq and sci-RNA-seq barcoded cells in plates without any instrument.
2018–19
Integration

title: Combining datasets
text:
As studies grew to many donors and batches, integration became essential: Seurat anchors (Stuart et al.), scVI, and Harmony (Korsunsky et al., Nature Methods 2019). Harmony was fast enough for a laptop and became one of the most widely used methods.
2020–22
Multiome and atlases

title: More layers, shared references
text:
Joint RNA + ATAC kits, nucleus-based protocols for frozen tissue, and reference atlases (Human Cell Atlas, Azimuth, CELLxGENE) made automated annotation practical.
2023–24
Fixed cells and millions

title: Probe-based and million-cell runs
text:
Fixed-RNA probe assays (10x Flex) separated sample collection from processing, which matters for clinical work. Split-pool kits reached millions of cells per experiment. Seurat v5 added on-disk data and sketching for this scale.
2025–26
Now

title: Perturbation atlases and foundation models
text: Datasets of up to ~100 million cells, such as large drug and CRISPR perturbation screens, train single-cell foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer and successors). The core workflow you will learn below (QC, normalisation, integration, clustering, annotation) is still the foundation for using them.

title: Single-cell platforms: advantages and limitations
text:
| Platform | How cells are barcoded | Advantages | Limitations | Cells per run
| 10x Chromium (3′, 5′, GEM-X) | Droplets with barcoded gel beads | Industry standard; Cell Ranger and broad tool support; 5′ adds immune receptor (TCR/BCR) sequencing | Needs fresh viable cells; instrument required; cost per cell | Thousands to ~1M with multiplexing
| 10x Flex | Probe hybridisation on fixed cells, then droplets | Fixed or FFPE samples; batch samples from many sites; high sensitivity | Targeted probe set; no isoforms or TCR/BCR | Up to hundreds of thousands, multiplexed
| Parse Evercode | Split-pool combinatorial barcoding in plates | No instrument; fixed cells; very large sample and cell numbers | Longer hands-on protocol; needs high cell input | Up to millions
| Scale Bio | Combinatorial indexing (split-pool) | Low cost per cell at scale | Smaller ecosystem | Up to millions
| BD Rhapsody | Microwells with barcoded beads | Gentle cell capture; targeted panels plus AbSeq proteins | Lower throughput than droplets | Tens of thousands
| Illumina Single Cell (PIPseq) | Particle-templated emulsion in a tube | No instrument; vortex-based; scalable | Newer, fewer published benchmarks | Thousands to ~1M
| Smart-seq3 (plate) | One cell per well | Full-length transcripts and isoforms; highest genes per cell | Low throughput; manual or robotic sorting | Hundreds
| Integration method | Approach | Strengths | Watch out for

title: Single-cell platforms: advantages and limitations
text:
| Harmony | Iterative soft clustering + linear correction in PCA space | Fast, memory-light, works on millions of cells, multiple batch variables | Corrects the embedding only, not the counts
| Seurat CCA / RPCA | Anchors between dataset pairs | Good for very different datasets (RPCA is faster) | Slower; CCA can over-correct
| scVI / scANVI | Variational autoencoder | Top performer on complex atlases; scANVI uses labels | Python, GPU helpful, more tuning
| fastMNN | Mutual nearest neighbours | Bioconductor-native | Order of batches matters

title: How Harmony works
text:
The same cell type looks slightly different in each batch. Differences in sample handling, chemistry, sequencing run or donor shift the cells in PCA space. If you cluster without correcting, you get "batch clusters" instead of cell-type clusters.
Harmony works on the PCA embedding and repeats two steps:
Soft clustering with a diversity penalty. Cells are softly assigned to clusters, and clusters made of only one batch are penalised. Strength is set by theta; higher means more mixing.
Correction. Within each cluster, every batch's centre is moved toward the cluster's overall centre, weighted by how strongly each cell belongs to that cluster.
It stops when the clusters stop changing. Because corrections are made per cluster, a cell type present in only one batch (the small purple group here) is not forced onto another type.
Move the slider through the iterations. Batch mixing rises while cell types stay separate.
Shape = batch (● batch 1, ▲ batch 2); colour = cell type. Purple type is rare in batch 2.
Batch mixing (kNN, higher = better)0.00
Cell-type purity (kNN, keep high)0.00
Note This is a 2-D teaching simulation of Harmony's algorithm. The real method runs on 20–50 principal components with the same logic.

title: Seurat pipeline: LogNormalize → Harmony → annotation
text: Uses the ifnb dataset from SeuratData: about 14,000 human PBMCs (Kang et al., 2018), half in a control batch and half stimulated with interferon-β. The stimulation shifts every cell type, a strong batch-like effect that integration has to handle without losing cell identity. The dataset ships with published annotations, so you can score your own annotation against them. Progress is saved in this browser.

Shell

# merge() keeps one counts layer per sample, ready for step 05

text:
R
InstallData("ifnb")
ifnb <- LoadData("ifnb")
ifnb <- UpdateSeuratObject(ifnb)
ifnb
table(ifnb$stim) # CTRL vs STIM: the batch variable
head(ifnb$seurat_annotations) # published labels: our answer key

title: Filter low-quality cells and doublets
text:
Remove dying cells (high mitochondrial fraction), empty or broken droplets (few genes), and doublets (two cells in one droplet). Choose thresholds per dataset from the plots, not from a fixed rule.
R
ifnb[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(ifnb, pattern = "^MT-")
VlnPlot(ifnb, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"),
group.by = "stim", pt.size = 0, ncol = 3)
FeatureScatter(ifnb, "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA", group.by = "stim")
ifnb <- subset(ifnb, subset = nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 &
percent.mt < 10)
# doublets, detected per sample
library(scDblFinder)
sce <- scDblFinder(as.SingleCellExperiment(ifnb), samples = "stim")
ifnb$doublet <- sce$scDblFinder.class
table(ifnb$doublet)
ifnb <- subset(ifnb, subset = doublet == "singlet")
ifnb The authors pre-filtered this dataset, so few cells are removed here and mitochondrial genes may be largely absent. On your own data, these filters matter a lot. Also consider ambient-RNA removal (SoupX, CellBender) for tissue samples.

title: Split by batch and LogNormalize
text:
We use Seurat's standard log-normalisation, not SCTransform. Each cell's counts are divided by its total, multiplied by 10,000, and log-transformed. It is simple, fast, transparent, and works well with Harmony. Splitting the RNA assay into one layer per batch lets Seurat select variable genes per batch.
R
ifnb[["RNA"]] <- split(ifnb[["RNA"]], f = ifnb$stim) # layers: counts.CTRL, counts.STIM
ifnb <- NormalizeData(ifnb, normalization.method = "LogNormalize",
scale.factor = 10000)
ifnb <- FindVariableFeatures(ifnb, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)
ifnb <- ScaleData(ifnb) # optional: vars.to.regress = "percent.mt"
Why not SCTransform? Both are valid. LogNormalize keeps one clear "data" layer that marker tests, ScType, SingleR and pseudobulk all use directly. SCTransform needs extra steps (PrepSCTFindMarkers) and more memory on large datasets.

title: PCA and choosing dimensions
text:
R
ifnb <- RunPCA(ifnb, npcs = 50)
ElbowPlot(ifnb, ndims = 50) # the curve flattens around 20–30 PCs
DimHeatmap(ifnb, dims = 1:6, cells = 500, balanced = TRUE)

title: Look at the data before integration
text:
Always look first. If CTRL and STIM cells form separate islands for the same cell type, integration is needed. If they already overlap, it may not be.
R
ifnb <- FindNeighbors(ifnb, dims = 1:30, reduction = "pca")
ifnb <- FindClusters(ifnb, resolution = 0.5, cluster.name = "unintegrated_clusters")
ifnb <- RunUMAP(ifnb, dims = 1:30, reduction = "pca",
reduction.name = "umap.unintegrated")
DimPlot(ifnb, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", group.by = c("stim", "seurat_annotations"))
Expect Each cell type splits into a CTRL island and a STIM island. That separation is the interferon response acting like a batch effect.

title: Integrate with Harmony
text:
Harmony takes the PCA embedding and returns a corrected embedding called harmony. Every downstream step (neighbours, clusters, UMAP) uses it instead of pca. Counts and the data layer are not changed.
R · Seurat v5 interface
ifnb <- IntegrateLayers(object = ifnb, method = HarmonyIntegration,
orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "harmony",
verbose = FALSE)
R · harmony package directly
# same result, with full control over parameters
ifnb <- RunHarmony(ifnb, group.by.vars = "stim", reduction.use = "pca",
dims.use = 1:30, theta = 2, reduction.save = "harmony")
# several batch variables, e.g. sample and chemistry:
# RunHarmony(obj, group.by.vars = c("sample", "chemistry"), theta = c(2, 1))
Which batch? Correct for technical variables (sample, lane, chemistry, donor). If you correct for your biological condition, as we do here for teaching, you must test condition effects later on the uncorrected data. Step 14 does that.

title: Cluster and visualise on the Harmony embedding
text:
R
ifnb <- FindNeighbors(ifnb, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30)
ifnb <- FindClusters(ifnb, resolution = 0.5, cluster.name = "harmony_clusters")
ifnb <- RunUMAP(ifnb, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30,
reduction.name = "umap.harmony")
DimPlot(ifnb, reduction = "umap.harmony",
group.by = c("stim", "harmony_clusters"), label = TRUE)
ifnb <- JoinLayers(ifnb) # merge CTRL/STIM layers back for marker testing
Resolution Try 0.3–1.2. Use clustree to see how clusters split as resolution rises. Pick the lowest value that separates the cell types you care about.

title: Check that integration worked
text:
Good integration mixes batches within clusters but keeps cell types apart. Check both, numerically.
R
# each cluster should contain both conditions
prop.table(table(ifnb$harmony_clusters, ifnb$stim), margin = 1) |> round(2)
# LISI: iLISI ≈ 2 means two batches fully mixed; cLISI ≈ 1 means types kept apart
remotes::install_github("immunogenomics/lisi")
meta <- ifnb@meta.data[, c("stim", "seurat_annotations")]
before <- lisi::compute_lisi(Embeddings(ifnb, "pca")[, 1:30], meta, colnames(meta))
after <- lisi::compute_lisi(Embeddings(ifnb, "harmony")[, 1:30], meta, colnames(meta))
sapply(list(before = before, after = after), colMeans)
Over-correction If clearly different cell types (for example CD4 T and NK cells) start to merge, lower theta or correct for fewer variables.

title: Find marker genes
text:
Markers are the evidence behind every label. FindConservedMarkers finds genes that mark a cluster in both conditions, so they reflect cell identity rather than the stimulation.

Idents(ifnb) <- "harmony_clusters"
markers <- FindAllMarkers(ifnb, only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.25, logfc.threshold = 0.5)
markers |> group_by(cluster) |> slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 5)
FindConservedMarkers(ifnb, ident.1 = "0", grouping.var = "stim") |> head()

"CD14", "LYZ", "FCGR3A", "FCER1A", "LILRA4", "PPBP", "HBB")

title: Annotate cell types with ScType, confirm with SingleR
text:
ScType scores each cluster against a curated database of positive and negative marker genes for a tissue. SingleR uses a different source of evidence: correlation with a labelled reference. Where the two agree and the markers from step 11 support it, the label is reliable. Where they disagree, look closer.
R · ScType
library(HGNChelper); library(openxlsx)
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IanevskiAleksandr/sc-type/master/R/gene_sets_prepare.R")
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IanevskiAleksandr/sc-type/master/R/sctype_score_.R")
db <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IanevskiAleksandr/sc-type/master/ScTypeDB_full.xlsx"
gs <- gene_sets_prepare(db, "Immune system") # tissue: Immune system, Brain, Liver, ...
# ScType needs scaled values for its marker genes
feats <- union(VariableFeatures(ifnb), intersect(unlist(gs$gs_positive), rownames(ifnb)))
ifnb <- ScaleData(ifnb, features = feats)
scaled <- as.matrix(LayerData(ifnb, assay = "RNA", layer = "scale.data"))
es <- sctype_score(scRNAseqData = scaled, scaled = TRUE,
gs = gs$gs_positive, gs2 = gs$gs_negative)
cl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(ifnb$harmony_clusters), function(k) {
cells <- colnames(ifnb)[ifnb$harmony_clusters == k]
s <- sort(rowSums(es[, cells, drop = FALSE]), decreasing = TRUE)
data.frame(cluster = k, type = names(s)[1], score = s[1], ncells = length(cells))
}))
cl$type[cl$score < cl$ncells / 4] <- "Unknown" # low-confidence clusters
ifnb$sctype <- cl$type[match(ifnb$harmony_clusters, cl$cluster)]
DimPlot(ifnb, reduction = "umap.harmony", group.by = "sctype", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE)

title: Annotate cell types with ScType, confirm with SingleR
text:
R · SingleR cross-check
library(SingleR); library(celldex)
ref <- celldex::MonacoImmuneData() # sorted human immune cells
pred <- SingleR(test = LayerData(ifnb, layer = "data"), ref = ref,
labels = ref$label.fine, clusters = ifnb$harmony_clusters)
ifnb$singler <- pred$labels[match(ifnb$harmony_clusters, rownames(pred))]
# compare both methods, and score against the published labels
table(ScType = ifnb$sctype, SingleR = ifnb$singler)
table(ScType = ifnb$sctype, Published = ifnb$seurat_annotations)
R · final labels
# use the agreed label; resolve disagreements from the DotPlot
ifnb$celltype <- ifnb$sctype
# e.g. ifnb$celltype[ifnb$harmony_clusters == "7"] <- "pDC"
Idents(ifnb) <- "celltype"
DimPlot(ifnb, reduction = "umap.harmony", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE) + NoLegend()
Also Azimuth (RunAzimuth(ifnb, reference = "pbmcref")) maps cells to a Seurat reference atlas. For a third, independent opinion, step 13 adds CellTypist. Use at least two lines of evidence for every label.

title: Annotate with CellTypist
text:
CellTypist (Domínguez Conde et al., Science 2022) predicts cell types with logistic-regression models pre-trained on large curated atlases, such as the immune models covering ~100 fine immune types across tissues. It gives every cell a label and a confidence score. With majority voting, it then gives each cluster the label most of its cells received; we pass our Harmony clusters for that. It runs in Python, so the workflow is: export from Seurat, annotate, import back.
R · 1. export counts and Harmony clusters
dir.create("celltypist", showWarnings = FALSE)
counts <- LayerData(ifnb, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts") # raw counts, layers joined (step 09)
Matrix::writeMM(counts, "celltypist/counts.mtx")
writeLines(rownames(counts), "celltypist/genes.txt")
writeLines(colnames(counts), "celltypist/cells.txt")
write.csv(data.frame(cell = colnames(ifnb), cluster = ifnb$harmony_clusters),
"celltypist/clusters.csv", row.names = FALSE)
Shell · 2. run CellTypist
pip install celltypist scanpy
python scripts/scrnaseq_celltypist.py --indir celltypist \
--models Immune_All_Low.pkl Immune_All_High.pkl
# Low = ~100 fine immune types; High = ~30 broad types.
# The script normalises to log1p(CP10k) (the input CellTypist expects; same as
# Seurat LogNormalize), runs majority voting on your clusters and writes
# celltypist/celltypist_<model>.csv: predicted_labels, majority_voting, conf_score
R · 3. import and compare
ct <- read.csv("celltypist/celltypist_Immune_All_Low.csv", row.names = 1)
ifnb$celltypist <- ct[colnames(ifnb), "majority_voting"]

title: Annotate with CellTypist
text:
ifnb$celltypist_conf <- ct[colnames(ifnb), "conf_score"]
DimPlot(ifnb, reduction = "umap.harmony", group.by = "celltypist",
label = TRUE, repel = TRUE) + NoLegend()
FeaturePlot(ifnb, "celltypist_conf", reduction = "umap.harmony") # low = uncertain
table(CellTypist = ifnb$celltypist, ScType = ifnb$sctype)
table(CellTypist = ifnb$celltypist, Published = ifnb$seurat_annotations)
| Method | Evidence | Strengths | Limitations
| ScType (step 12) | Curated positive and negative marker genes | Fast, transparent, many tissues, R | Only as good as its marker lists; per cluster
| SingleR (step 12) | Correlation with labelled reference profiles | Per cell; any reference you supply | Reference must match your tissue
| CellTypist | Pre-trained classifier on large atlases | Fine immune subtypes, confidence scores, majority voting; you can train your own model | Python step; models mostly human, so check one exists for your tissue and species
| Azimuth | Mapping onto a Seurat reference atlas | Hierarchical labels, R | Limited set of references
Good to know Human PBMC data like ifnb suit Immune_All_Low/High; list all models with celltypist.models.models_description(). Model files download from the CellTypist server on first use, so that run needs internet. To use a model file of your own, give it with a path (./my_model.pkl); the script handles this, because CellTypist treats a bare name as a built-in model. title: Compare conditions within each cell type
text:
Integration helped us find matching cell types; now test the stimulation within each one. Tests use the normalised expression values, never the Harmony embedding. With biological replicates, use pseudobulk: sum counts per donor, condition and cell type, then run limma-voom with TMM, exactly as in Module 1.
R · teaching (ifnb has no donor IDs)
ifnb$celltype.stim <- paste(ifnb$celltype, ifnb$stim, sep = "_")
Idents(ifnb) <- "celltype.stim"
mono_ifn <- FindMarkers(ifnb, ident.1 = "Classical Monocytes_STIM", # use your label names
ident.2 = "Classical Monocytes_CTRL")
head(mono_ifn, 10) # expect interferon genes: ISG15, IFIT1, IFI6, MX1
FeaturePlot(ifnb, c("ISG15", "CXCL10"), split.by = "stim", reduction = "umap.harmony")
R · real studies: pseudobulk + limma-voom
library(edgeR); library(limma)
# obj needs three separate columns: celltype, donor_id (the person or animal),
# and condition. One pseudobulk sample = one donor x condition x cell type.
pb <- AggregateExpression(obj, assays = "RNA", return.seurat = TRUE,
group.by = c("celltype", "donor_id", "condition"))
md <- pb@meta.data # keeps celltype, donor_id, condition per column
unique(md$celltype) # Seurat may change "_" to "-" in labels
sel <- md$celltype == "CD14 Mono"
y <- DGEList(LayerData(pb, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")[, sel])
info <- data.frame(donor = factor(md$donor_id[sel]),
condition = factor(md$condition[sel], levels = c("CTRL", "STIM")))
y <- y[filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- calcNormFactors(y, method = "TMM")
# paired design: each donor measured in both conditions

title: Compare conditions within each cell type
text:
design <- model.matrix(~ donor + condition, data = info)
# (different donors per condition: design <- model.matrix(~ condition, data = info))
fit <- eBayes(lmFit(voom(y, design), design))
topTable(fit, coef = "conditionSTIM", n = 20)
Tested On simulated data with 4 donors × 2 conditions, this gives 8 pseudobulk samples per cell type and ranks all 30 planted interferon genes first. Grouping by donor alone would have merged each donor's control and stimulated cells into one sample.
Don't Treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates significance hugely (pseudoreplication). For publication-grade condition comparisons, use pseudobulk across donors.

title: Glossary
text:
UMI
Unique molecular identifier: a random barcode on each captured molecule, so PCR duplicates are counted once.
Doublet
A droplet that captured two cells; it looks like a hybrid cell type.
LogNormalize
log1p(count / cell total × 10,000): Seurat's default normalisation.
Batch effect
Technical variation between groups of samples processed differently.
theta (Harmony)
Diversity penalty strength; higher values push harder for batch mixing.
LISI
Local inverse Simpson's index: the effective number of batches (iLISI) or cell types (cLISI) around each cell.
Pseudobulk
Summing counts over cells of one type per sample, giving proper replicates for DE testing.

title: What is spatial omics?
text:
Single-cell RNA-seq tells you which cells are in a sample and what they express, but it dissociates the tissue first, so every cell's location is lost. Spatial omics measures RNA (and increasingly protein) in place, on an intact tissue section. Each measurement keeps its x/y coordinate.
That coordinate is what makes new questions answerable. Which immune cells actually touch the tumour? Is a fibroblast state confined to the invasive margin? Do two cell types always appear together in the same micro-environment? These are questions about neighbourhoods, and you can only ask them when location is preserved.

title: Imaging-based (in situ)
text:
Fluorescent probes bind target RNAs directly in the tissue. A microscope images the slide over many cycles, and each transcript's colour code is decoded into a gene name and a position.
Single-cell and subcellular resolution
Targeted gene panels (hundreds to a few thousand genes; some now reach whole transcriptome)
Examples: Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE

title: Sequencing-based (capture)
text:
Transcripts are captured onto a slide covered in spatially barcoded spots or bins. The library is sequenced, and the barcode tells you where each read came from.
Unbiased whole transcriptome
Resolution set by spot or bin size (55 µm down to 2 µm or less)
Examples: Visium / Visium HD, Stereo-seq, Curio Seeker

title: Xenium analysis pipeline in R
text: Built on the 10x Genomics Xenium downstream analysis in R guide (Seurat v5, BPCells sketching, Harmony, Banksy), with extra steps for quality control, re-segmentation, reference-based annotation and niche analysis. Tick steps off as you go; your progress is saved in this browser.

title: Install the R toolkit
text:
Seurat v5 reads Xenium bundles directly. BPCells keeps large matrices on disk so a 1M-cell Prime 5K run fits on a laptop. Harmony corrects batch effects; Banksy adds spatially aware clustering; spacexr gives reference-based cell typing.
R
# R ≥ 4.3 recommended
install.packages(c("Seurat", "remotes", "arrow", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "harmony"))
remotes::install_github("bnprks/BPCells/r") # on-disk matrices
remotes::install_github("satijalab/seurat-wrappers") # RunBanksy()
remotes::install_github("prabhakarlab/Banksy")
remotes::install_github("dmcable/spacexr") # RCTD annotation
library(Seurat); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
options(future.globals.maxSize = 8 * 1024^3) # 8 GB for big objects
Compute A Xenium v1 run (~300k cells) needs ~32 GB RAM. A Prime 5K run with ~1M cells is comfortable at 64–128 GB, or use the sketch workflow in step 09. On AWS that is roughly an r6i.2xlarge to r6i.4xlarge instance.

title: Get the data and learn the output bundle
text:
Download the Xenium Prime 5K Human Breast Cancer (FFPE) dataset from the 10x Datasets page (filter by Xenium). Unzip it and you get the outs/ folder the instrument produces. Knowing these files matters more than any one package.
outs/
├── experiment.xenium # run metadata; open this in Xenium Explorer
├── metrics_summary.csv # run-level QC: median transcripts/cell, decoded counts
├── cell_feature_matrix.h5 # cells × genes counts (plus control probes/codewords)
├── cells.parquet # per-cell centroid, area, nucleus area, counts
├── transcripts.parquet # every decoded transcript: gene, x, y, z, qv, cell_id
├── cell_boundaries.parquet # segmentation polygons
├── nucleus_boundaries.parquet
├── morphology_focus/ # DAPI + multimodal segmentation stain images (OME-TIFF)
└── analysis/ # instrument's own clustering, UMAP, DE
Shell
# paste the "Output files" link from the dataset page
curl -O "<URL of the Xenium output bundle .zip>"
unzip Xenium_Prime_Human_Breast_*_outs.zip -d breast_5k
head -5 breast_5k/outs/metrics_summary.csv
Tip Some older tools want transcripts.csv.gz. Convert with arrow::read_parquet("transcripts.parquet") |> data.table::fwrite("transcripts.csv.gz"). Recent Seurat reads Parquet directly.

title: Load Xenium into Seurat
text:
LoadXenium() builds a Seurat object with the gene counts, cell centroids, segmentation boundaries and transcript coordinates in one spatial "field of view" (FOV). Low-quality transcripts (QV < 20) are dropped at import.
R
xen <- LoadXenium("breast_5k/outs", fov = "fov", assay = "Xenium")
xen
Assays(xen) # Xenium + BlankCodeword / ControlCodeword / ControlProbe
# add per-cell morphology (area) from cells.parquet
cells <- arrow::read_parquet("breast_5k/outs/cells.parquet")
xen$cell_area <- cells$cell_area[match(colnames(xen), cells$cell_id)]
xen$nucleus_area <- cells$nucleus_area[match(colnames(xen), cells$cell_id)]

title: Quality control: cells, controls and run metrics
text:
Imaging data has its own failure modes: empty segmentations, tiny debris "cells", and off-target signal. Negative-control probes and blank codewords estimate the false-positive rate. Thresholds depend on panel size, so look at the distributions before you choose cutoffs.
R
VlnPlot(xen, features = c("nFeature_Xenium", "nCount_Xenium", "cell_area"),
ncol = 3, pt.size = 0)
# false-positive estimate: control signal relative to real genes
ctrl <- colSums(LayerData(xen, assay = "ControlProbe", layer = "counts")) +
colSums(LayerData(xen, assay = "BlankCodeword", layer = "counts"))
xen$pct_control <- 100 * ctrl / (xen$nCount_Xenium + ctrl)
summary(xen$pct_control) # aim for a median well under 1%
# filter: thresholds for a 5K panel; use ~10 counts / 5 genes for a ~300-gene panel
xen <- subset(xen, subset = nCount_Xenium >= 50 & nFeature_Xenium >= 25 &
pct_control < 5 & cell_area > 10)
ncol(xen)
Checkpoint Compare your median transcripts per cell with metrics_summary.csv. Map the removed cells with ImageDimPlot(): if they cluster in one region, suspect a tissue fold or detachment, not biology.

title: Re-segment cells if boundaries look wrong
text:
Every downstream result inherits the segmentation. Nuclear expansion can assign one cell's transcripts to its neighbour, which shows up as "doublet" clusters such as T cells expressing epithelial keratins. Recent runs use multimodal segmentation (boundary, interior and nuclear stains). For older data, or crowded tissue, re-segment.
Shell
# Xenium Ranger (free from 10x): change nuclear expansion distance
xeniumranger resegment --id=breast_reseg \
--xenium-bundle=breast_5k/outs --expansion-distance=5
# or import a segmentation made elsewhere (Cellpose, Baysor, Proseg)
xeniumranger import-segmentation --id=breast_cellpose \
--xenium-bundle=breast_5k/outs --cells=cellpose_masks.tif
2025–26 trend Transcript-based segmenters (Proseg, Baysor, segger) place cell boundaries using the transcripts themselves, not just the stain. They usually reduce contamination between neighbouring cells. Compare marker co-expression before and after to judge the gain.

title: Normalise, reduce and cluster
text:
Targeted panels are not a random sample of the transcriptome, so use every gene as a feature rather than picking variable genes. SCTransform handles the depth differences between small and large cells well.
R
xen <- SCTransform(xen, assay = "Xenium")
xen <- RunPCA(xen, npcs = 30, features = rownames(xen))
ElbowPlot(xen, ndims = 30)
xen <- RunUMAP(xen, dims = 1:30)
xen <- FindNeighbors(xen, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:30)
xen <- FindClusters(xen, resolution = 0.3)
DimPlot(xen, label = TRUE) + NoLegend()
Choose For >500k cells, SCTransform gets slow. Use NormalizeData() + ScaleData(), or the sketch workflow in step 09. Try resolutions from 0.2 to 1.0; with 5,000 genes you can resolve finer subtypes than with a 300-gene panel.

title: Plot clusters and transcripts on the tissue
text:
This is where spatial pays off. Put clusters back on the slide, then crop a region of interest and overlay individual transcripts with the segmentation outlines to check that clusters match morphology.
R
ImageDimPlot(xen, fov = "fov", cols = "polychrome", size = 0.6, axes = TRUE)
ImageFeaturePlot(xen, features = c("EPCAM", "PTPRC", "ACTA2", "PECAM1"),
max.cutoff = "q90", size = 0.6)
# zoom into a region of interest (coordinates in microns)
xen[["zoom"]] <- Crop(xen[["fov"]], x = c(1200, 2900), y = c(3750, 4550),
coords = "plot")
DefaultBoundary(xen[["zoom"]]) <- "segmentation"
ImageDimPlot(xen, fov = "zoom", cols = "polychrome", coord.fixed = FALSE,
border.color = "white", border.size = 0.1,
molecules = c("EPCAM", "PTPRC", "ACTA2", "PECAM1"), nmols = 20000)

title: Find markers and annotate cell types
text:
Start with marker genes per cluster, as in the 10x guide. Then confirm with a reference: label transfer from a matched scRNA-seq atlas is now standard and catches mixed clusters that markers alone miss.
R · markers
xen <- PrepSCTFindMarkers(xen)
markers <- FindAllMarkers(xen, only.pos = TRUE, logfc.threshold = 0.25, min.pct = 0.1)
top5 <- markers |> group_by(cluster) |> slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 5)
DotPlot(xen, features = unique(top5$gene)) + RotatedAxis()
# name clusters from markers (example map; fill in from your DotPlot)
labels <- c("0" = "Tumour epithelium", "1" = "CAF", "2" = "Macrophage",
"3" = "T cell", "4" = "Endothelial", "5" = "B / plasma")
xen$celltype <- unname(labels[as.character(xen$seurat_clusters)])
R · reference (RCTD)
library(spacexr)
# ref_seurat: a matched scRNA-seq reference with a "celltype" column
ref <- Reference(LayerData(ref_seurat, layer = "counts"),
factor(ref_seurat$celltype))
coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(xen[["fov"]], which = "centroids")
rownames(coords) <- coords$cell
query <- SpatialRNA(coords[, c("x", "y")],
LayerData(xen, assay = "Xenium", layer = "counts"))
rctd <- create.RCTD(query, ref, max_cores = 8, UMI_min = 20)
rctd <- run.RCTD(rctd, doublet_mode = "doublet") # models 1–2 types per cell
res <- rctd@results$results_df
xen$rctd_type <- as.character(res$first_type[match(colnames(xen), rownames(res))])
Export Load labels back into Xenium Explorer: write.csv(data.frame(cell_id = colnames(xen), group = xen$celltype), "celltypes.csv", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE), then Cell → Add cell categorization.

title: Integrate several samples with sketching and Harmony
text:
Two Prime 5K slides can exceed a million cells. The 10x guide keeps the full matrices on disk with BPCells, learns structure on a 50,000-cell "sketch", corrects batch effects with Harmony, then projects the result back onto every cell.
R
library(BPCells)
samples <- c(breast = "breast_5k/outs", cervix = "cervix_5k/outs")
mats <- lapply(names(samples), function(s) {
m <- open_matrix_10x_hdf5(file.path(samples[[s]], "cell_feature_matrix.h5"),
feature_type = "Gene Expression")
colnames(m) <- paste0(s, "_", colnames(m)) # unique cell IDs
write_matrix_dir(m, dir = file.path("bpcells", s), overwrite = TRUE)
open_matrix_dir(file.path("bpcells", s))
})
names(mats) <- names(samples)
obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = mats) # one layer per sample
obj$sample <- sub("_.*", "", colnames(obj))
obj <- NormalizeData(obj) |> FindVariableFeatures()
obj <- SketchData(obj, ncells = 50000, method = "LeverageScore",
sketched.assay = "sketch")
DefaultAssay(obj) <- "sketch"
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj) |> ScaleData() |> RunPCA(npcs = 30)
obj <- IntegrateLayers(obj, method = HarmonyIntegration,
orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "harmony")
obj <- FindNeighbors(obj, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30) |>
FindClusters(resolution = 0.5)
obj <- RunUMAP(obj, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30, return.model = TRUE)
# project sketch → all cells
obj <- ProjectIntegration(obj, sketched.assay = "sketch", assay = "RNA",
reduction = "harmony")
obj <- ProjectData(obj, sketched.assay = "sketch", assay = "RNA",
sketched.reduction = "harmony.full", full.reduction = "harmony.full",

title: Integrate several samples with sketching and Harmony
text:
dims = 1:30, refdata = list(cluster_full = "seurat_clusters"))
# UMAP of ALL cells from the projected Harmony embedding
obj <- RunUMAP(obj, reduction = "harmony.full", dims = 1:30,
reduction.name = "umap.full", reduction.key = "UMAPfull_")
DefaultAssay(obj) <- "RNA"
DimPlot(obj, reduction = "umap.full", group.by = c("sample", "cluster_full"))
Then Subset to one compartment (for example macrophages) and re-cluster to find states such as SPP1⁺ versus C1Q⁺ tumour-associated macrophages. This is the final section of the 10x guide.

title: Find tissue domains with Banksy
text:
Standard clustering ignores location. Banksy adds each cell's neighbourhood expression to its own. With a low λ it refines cell types; with a high λ it finds tissue domains such as tumour core, invasive margin, stroma and tertiary lymphoid structures.
R
library(SeuratWrappers); library(Banksy)
cent <- GetTissueCoordinates(xen[["fov"]], which = "centroids")
xen$sx <- cent$x[match(colnames(xen), cent$cell)]
xen$sy <- cent$y[match(colnames(xen), cent$cell)]
xen <- RunBanksy(xen, lambda = 0.8, assay = "SCT", slot = "data",
features = "all", dimx = "sx", dimy = "sy", k_geom = 30)
xen <- RunPCA(xen, assay = "BANKSY", reduction.name = "pca.banksy",
features = rownames(xen), npcs = 30)
xen <- FindNeighbors(xen, reduction = "pca.banksy", dims = 1:30)
xen <- FindClusters(xen, resolution = 0.5, cluster.name = "banksy_domain")
ImageDimPlot(xen, group.by = "banksy_domain", cols = "polychrome", size = 0.6)
λ guide lambda = 0.2 for cell typing; lambda = 0.8 for domains. Alternatives worth knowing: CellCharter, and the deep-learning model Novae.

title: Cellular niches and neighbourhood enrichment
text:
A niche is defined by which cell types surround a cell. Seurat counts the annotated types among each cell's 30 nearest neighbours and clusters those compositions. Then test which pairs of cell types sit together more often than chance.
R

niches.k = 6, neighbors.k = 30)
ImageDimPlot(xen, group.by = "niches", size = 0.6, dark.background = FALSE)
# composition of each niche
table(xen$celltype, xen$niches) |> prop.table(margin = 2) |> round(2)

title: Multi-slide TMA project: from two slides to per-animal statistics
text:
The tutorial above analyses one tissue section. Real projects are messier. This case study is a general version of the pipeline used in an actual project: two Xenium slides, each a tissue microarray (TMA) of mouse tissue cores, with several cores per animal and every group spread over both slides. It covers the decisions the tutorial doesn't, and the full script is ready to adapt.
Hundreds of thousands of cells Too many for in-memory clustering: sketch 25k cells per slide
Dozens of cores per slide No core IDs in the Xenium output: detect them, then match them to the TMA map
Replicate = animal Cores from one animal are not independent; cells even less so
Groups on both slides Then slide is a batch you can check, not a confounder. The script verifies it.

title: DBSCAN, merge fragments, drop debris
text:
DBSCAN on cell centroids (eps = 75 µm) finds dense tissue islands. Pieces of a torn core whose centres are closer than 800 µm are merged; groups under 300 cells are debris. A labelled core-map PDF lets you check every core by eye.
2 · Match to the TMA map

title: Try all 8 orientations
text:
Slides are often scanned rotated or mirrored relative to the paper map. The script infers the grid from the core centres, tries all 8 rotations and mirror images, and keeps the one where the map's Empty spots fall on missing cores. Cores then carry stable map numbers (P01, P02, …), and a lost core is reported, not silently matched.
3 · Curated files with safety checks

title: No statistics until metadata and labels are verified
text:
core_map.csv (animal, condition, exclude) is pre-filled from the map and stores each core's centre. If a later run detects cores differently, mismatched IDs are flagged. Composition and DE tests only run once every kept core has an animal ID and the cluster labels are marked reviewed.
4 · Design check

title: Is every group on both slides?
text:
The script tabulates condition × slide. With groups spread over slides, slide is an ordinary batch: check the UMAP by slide, and use Harmony only if the same cell types separate by slide. If a group sits on one slide only, the script warns that group and slide effects cannot be separated and the results are exploratory.
5 · QC per slide, explained per core

title: Know why each core lost cells
text:
≥ 20 transcripts and ≥ 15 genes; controls ≤ 5% of counts; upper count and area cut-offs computed per slide (merged cells). qc_per_core.csv counts each failure reason per core, so a folded core is fixed at the cause, not by loosening the thresholds for everyone.
6 · Panel-aware annotation

title: Markers that are actually on the panel
text:
Many textbook markers (Krt14, Krt5, Krt10, Lor, Acta2, Lyz2, Dcn, …) are not on the Xenium Mouse 5K panel. The script reports marker coverage, scores clusters, and calls a cluster Ambiguous when the top two scores are close. Your reviewed labels are tied to a fingerprint of the clustering, so they can never land on different cells after a re-run.
7 · Niches that stay inside a core

title: Neighbours from the same core only
text:
Neighbourhood profiles use the 30 nearest cells within 100 µm, from the same core only, then are clustered jointly over all cores so niche labels are comparable. For Banksy, cores are shifted far apart before the neighbour search for the same reason.
8 · Statistics per animal

title: Composition test and pseudobulk DE
text: Cell-type proportions per animal are compared with logit-transformed proportions and limma (the speckle/propeller idea). Pseudobulk sums counts per cell type × animal × condition for DESeq2, with ~ mouse_id + condition when the same animal gives both conditions. Unassigned clusters and under-powered cell types are skipped, and the reason is written down.

Label matching tested on the published files Not yet run end to end
RCTD labels each Xenium cell by comparing it with a single-cell reference from the same tissue. The companion script builds one from GSE129218 (Joost et al. 2020, full-thickness mouse skin). By default it uses the cell types the original authors assigned, downloaded from their public GitHub repository. Label transfer is then independent of your own annotation: if RCTD agrees with your marker-based labels, two separate lines of evidence agree.
| Broad label | From the authors' categories | Cells (author files, before QC)
| Basal_Proliferating_KC | IFE B, IFE C | 1,154
| Differentiated_KC | IFE SB1, IFE SB2 | 773
| HairFollicle_KC | other epidermal + all anagen follicle layers | 2,830
| Fibroblast | FIB1–4, dermal sheath, dermal papilla | 385
| Macrophage_DC | MC1–3, DC, LC | 182
| Endothelial · Melanocyte · Skeletal muscle · Sebocyte · T cell | EC1–2 · MEL1–2 · SM · SG · TC | 123 · 125 · 41 · 28 · 28

After the first run: 10-step checklist
Cores: open cores/*_core_map.pdf and *_core_map_matched.pdf; compare a few cores with the H&E. The chosen orientation in *_orientations.csv should have 0 mismatches.
Metadata: check curated/core_map.csv; every kept core needs an animal, condition and stratum; set exclude for folded cores. condition_by_slide.csv should show every group on both slides.
QC: read qc/qc_per_core.csv; fix causes before changing thresholds, and keep one rule for all samples.
Batch: UMAP by slide; the same cell types should overlap. Add Harmony only if they don't.
Labels: compare module scores, marker dot plot, markers and spatial plots (plus RCTD); edit curated/cluster_labels.csv, keep doubtful clusters Unassigned/Ambiguous, set reviewed = TRUE, re-run.
Explorer: load explorer/*.csv and check labels on DAPI / H&E.
Niches: name niches from the heatmap; only keep niches that stay stable when you change NICHE_K and N_NICHES.
Statistics then run automatically: composition test, pseudobulk DE, and a file saying which cell types were skipped and why. Aim for ≥ 3 animals per group.
Pathways: use the panel genes as the background, not the whole genome.
Methods: each run folder keeps its settings, session info and the curated files it used.

title: Downstream analyses: composition, space and genes
text: Once cores are matched, animals assigned and labels reviewed, three kinds of question remain. Which cell types change? How is the tissue organised? Which genes and pathways respond? The rule is the same throughout: the animal is the replicate, never the cell or the core. Every test below uses one value per animal (or per animal and condition). The code reads the object saved by the case-study script; the column names are those in core_map.csv.

title: A1 · Treatment effect over time, adjusted for slide
text:
Count each cell type per animal, turn counts into proportions, and logit-transform them so a linear model fits (the speckle/propeller idea). With different animals per group, the model asks three questions:
Overall: is a cell type changed by treatment, after allowing for slide and time point?
Per time point: treated vs control at each time.
Over time: does the treatment effect itself change? This is the time × treatment interaction.
R · A1
library(limma)
# one sample per animal (x condition): logit cell-type proportions + sample table
per_animal <- function(m) {
m$sample <- paste(m$mouse_id, m$condition, sep = "|")
cnt <- as.matrix(as.data.frame.matrix(table(m$sample, m$celltype)))
samp <- m[!duplicated(m$sample), c("sample", "mouse_id", "condition", "stratum", "slide")]
list(y = t(qlogis((cnt + 0.5) / rowSums(cnt + 0.5))),
samp = samp[match(rownames(cnt), samp$sample), ])
}
a <- per_animal(md[md$condition %in% c("control", "treated"), ])
a$samp$condition <- factor(a$samp$condition, levels = c("control", "treated"))
# overall effect, adjusted for slide and time
d1 <- model.matrix(~ slide + stratum + condition, a$samp)
topTable(eBayes(lmFit(a$y, d1), robust = TRUE), coef = "conditiontreated")
# does the effect change over time? (interaction, F-test)
d2 <- model.matrix(~ slide + stratum * condition, a$samp)
topTable(eBayes(lmFit(a$y, d2), robust = TRUE), coef = grep(":", colnames(d2)))

title: A2 · Progression within the same animal (paired)
text:
When one animal provides an early and an advanced lesion, compare each animal with itself. Adding the animal to the model removes the large differences between animals, so smaller shifts become visible. Only animals with both stages are used. To pool stages first (e.g. two advanced stages), relabel them before counting.
R · A2
p <- per_animal(md[md$condition %in% c("early_lesion", "advanced_lesion"), ])
both <- names(which(table(p$samp$mouse_id) == 2)) # complete pairs only
keep <- p$samp$mouse_id %in% both
ps <- droplevels(p$samp[keep, ])
ps$condition <- factor(ps$condition, levels = c("early_lesion", "advanced_lesion"))
d <- model.matrix(~ mouse_id + condition, ps) # animal as a block
fit <- eBayes(lmFit(p$y[, keep], d), robust = TRUE)
topTable(fit, coef = "conditionadvanced_lesion")
Proportions add up to 100% If one cell type expands, every other type's share falls, even when its cell numbers don't change. In our test, rising T cells made fibroblasts look like they fell over time. Read a drop in a large population next to the rise that caused it, and confirm key results with a ratio (e.g. T cells per epithelial cell) or cells per mm² of tissue.

title: B1 · Who sits next to whom
text:
For each core, count each cell type's neighbours (here the 10 nearest cells), then shuffle the cell-type labels within the core many times. The z-score says whether type B sits next to type A more (z > 0) or less (z < 0) often than chance. Average per animal, then compare groups. This is how you test, for example, whether T cells move into contact with the epithelium.
R · B1
z_core <- function(xy, ct, k = 10, nperm = 200) {
ct <- factor(ct); nn <- dbscan::kNN(xy, k = k)$id
tab <- function(l) as.matrix(table(factor(rep(l, k), levels(ct)),
factor(l[as.vector(nn)], levels(ct))))
obs <- tab(ct); perm <- replicate(nperm, tab(sample(ct))) # shuffle within the core
(obs - apply(perm, 1:2, mean)) / apply(perm, 1:2, sd)
}
d <- md[md$sample_id == "TMA1_P01", ]
z <- z_core(as.matrix(d[, c("x_centroid", "y_centroid")]), d$celltype)
z["T_cell", "Basal_KC"] # > 2: T cells contact basal cells more than by chance

title: B2 · Immune infiltration and the epithelium–stroma interface
text:
Measure distances, not just counts. For every immune cell, take the distance to the nearest epithelial (or tumour) cell. Infiltration is the fraction of immune cells within, say, 30 µm. The interface is the band of cells within 30 µm of both epithelium and stroma, which is where tumour–stroma contact happens. Summarise per animal and test with the same design as A1.
R · B2
xy <- as.matrix(d[, c("x_centroid", "y_centroid")])
epi <- d$celltype %in% c("Basal_KC", "Differentiated_KC")
str <- d$celltype %in% c("Fibroblast", "Endothelial")
imm <- d$celltype %in% c("T_cell", "Macrophage")
d_epi <- dbscan::kNN(xy[epi, ], k = 1, query = xy)$dist[, 1] # to nearest epithelial cell
d_str <- dbscan::kNN(xy[str, ], k = 1, query = xy)$dist[, 1]
mean(d_epi[imm] <= 30) # immune infiltration
interface <- d_epi <= 30 & d_str <= 30 # epithelium–stroma interface
mean(imm[interface]) # immune share at the interface
# repeat per core, average per animal, then lm(metric ~ slide + stratum + condition)

title: B3 · Tissue layering: epidermis to dermis
text:
Use the basal layer as a ruler. Bin every other cell by its distance from the nearest basal cell (0–25, 25–50, 50–100 µm, …) and plot the cell-type mix per bin. In normal skin the profile runs from differentiated keratinocytes above, through the basal layer, into fibroblast-rich dermis. A flattened profile is a quantitative sign of disorganisation. For data-driven tissue domains, use the niches or Banksy from the case-study script.
R · B3
bas <- d$celltype == "Basal_KC"
d$d_basal <- dbscan::kNN(xy[bas, ], k = 1, query = xy)$dist[, 1]
d$bin <- cut(d$d_basal, c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf), include.lowest = TRUE)
prop.table(table(d$bin[!bas], d$celltype[!bas]), 1) |> round(2)

title: C1 · Pseudobulk DE per cell type
text:
Sum the raw counts of each cell type per animal (and condition), then run DESeq2 with the same designs as A: ~ slide + stratum + condition for treatment, ~ mouse_id + condition for paired progression. Cell types with too few animals, or fewer than 20 cells per animal, are skipped with the reason recorded.
R · C1
counts <- LayerData(obj, "counts", assay = "Xenium")
kc <- md[md$celltype == "Basal_KC" & md$condition %in% c("control", "treated"), ]
f <- factor(paste(kc$mouse_id, kc$condition, sep = "|")) # same sample ids as A1
pb <- as.matrix(counts[, rownames(kc)] %*% Matrix::sparse.model.matrix(~ 0 + f))
colnames(pb) <- levels(f) # genes x animals
info <- a$samp[match(colnames(pb), a$samp$sample), ]; rownames(info) <- info$sample
dds <- DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(pb, info, ~ slide + stratum + condition)
dds <- DESeq2::DESeq(dds)
res <- DESeq2::results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "treated", "control"))

title: C2 · Pathways: p53, DNA repair, inflammation
text:
Rank the tested genes by the DESeq2 statistic and run GSEA on MSigDB Hallmark sets: P53_PATHWAY, DNA_REPAIR, UV_RESPONSE_UP, INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE, TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB, G2M_CHECKPOINT. Cut each set to the genes on your panel first: a 5K panel holds only part of each set, and the background must be the panel, not the genome. A per-cell pathway score, averaged per animal, makes the result easy to plot.
R · C2
h <- msigdbr::msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "H")
sets <- split(h$gene_symbol, h$gs_name)[c("HALLMARK_P53_PATHWAY", "HALLMARK_DNA_REPAIR",
"HALLMARK_INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE")]
st <- sort(setNames(res$stat, rownames(res))[!is.na(res$stat)], decreasing = TRUE)
sets <- lapply(sets, intersect, names(st)) # panel genes only
fgsea::fgsea(sets[lengths(sets) >= 5], st, minSize = 5) # NES > 0: up in treated
# per-cell score = mean z-score of the set's panel genes; then average per animal
g <- intersect(sets$HALLMARK_P53_PATHWAY, rownames(obj))
x <- as.matrix(LayerData(obj, "data", assay = "Xenium")[g, ])
md$p53_score <- colMeans((x - rowMeans(x)) / apply(x, 1, sd))

title: Glossary
text:
FOV
Field of view: one imaged tile, or in Seurat the spatial container holding coordinates and boundaries.
QV
Phred-style quality score for a decoded transcript. QV 20 means about a 1% chance the gene call is wrong.
Codeword
The sequence of colours across imaging cycles that identifies a gene. Blank codewords match no gene and measure decoding errors.
Segmentation
Drawing cell boundaries so that transcripts can be assigned to cells.
Sketching
Analysing a representative subsample of cells, then projecting results onto all cells.
Niche
A recurring local mix of cell types, for example tumour cells next to SPP1⁺ macrophages and CAFs.
Bin
In sequencing-based platforms, a square of barcodes aggregated into one unit (for example 8 × 8 µm in Visium HD).
